name: Forrester v. City of San Diego
court: Ninth Circuit (from the Southern District of California)
topic: Fourth Amendment excessive force, pain compliance holds and Orcutt Police Nunchakus on passively resisting demonstrators, no least intrusive alternative requirement, municipal policy
summary: San Diego police used pain compliance techniques, including a wrist device the court called Orcutt Police Nonchakus, to move anti-abortion demonstrators who sat, went limp, and refused to leave medical clinics. A jury that watched the videotape found no excessive force, and the Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that officers are not required to use the least intrusive degree of force possible. The court did not decide whether the city's pain compliance policy was constitutional, and a dissent would have held the force unreasonable as a matter of law. It is taught as the anchor case for pain compliance on passive resisters.
coverage: The full opinion, including Judge Kleinfeld's dissent and all footnotes, was read from the Public.Resource.Org Federal Reporter archive at https://law.resource.org/pub/us/case/reporter/F3/025/25.F3d.804.92-55137.html. The archive file is headed 25 F.3d 804 and carries docket No. 92-55137, which confirms the citation.

The archive text has paragraph numbers but no Federal Reporter page breaks, so no pin cites are given. The majority's internal references to the dissent (for example "Dissent at 812") indicate the opinion runs at least to page 812.
The district court proceedings, the magistrate judge's summary judgment ruling on the policy, and the videotape are described only as the Ninth Circuit described them.
No subsequent history was verified for this brief.
The court spelled the wrist device "Orcutt Police Nonchakus" (OPNs). Course materials use the common spelling nunchakus. Both refer to the same device.

Course materials sometimes describe Forrester as holding that pain compliance on passive resisters "was objectively reasonable." The court's actual holding is narrower: substantial evidence supported a jury verdict that the force was reasonable. The dissent emphasized that the majority did not hold pain compliance permissible as a matter of law, and the majority expressly declined to decide whether the city's policy was constitutional.
facts:
In March 1989, San Diego police learned that Operation Rescue planned several anti-abortion demonstrations in the city. Police Chief Burgreen met with his staff and adopted a plan for dispersing and arresting demonstrators who trespassed on and blocked the entrances to private medical clinics.

The plan had three steps. Officers would first give protesters a verbal warning and an opportunity to leave. Officers would then arrest those who refused and give them another chance to move on their own. Finally, officers would remove the remaining demonstrators with "pain compliance techniques," meaning the application of pain as needed to make them move. The policy allowed either Orcutt Police Nonchakus (two wooden sticks joined at one end by a cord, used to grip a wrist) or direct physical contact such as a firm grip, wrist and arm twisting, and pressure point holds.

San Diego officers normally had discretion to use either pain compliance or drag and carry. For these demonstrations the chief absolutely prohibited drag and carry. He gave two reasons: preventing the back injuries that repeated dragging and carrying causes to officers and arrestees, and maximizing police control over the large crowds he expected.

At each of the three demonstrations at issue, protesters converged on a medical building, blocked entrances, filled stairwells and corridors, and kept employees and patients from entering. When police or property owners tried to remove them, the demonstrators resisted passively by staying seated, refusing to move, and refusing to bear weight. At the first demonstration the first officers on scene dragged and carried arrestees. After the pain compliance unit arrived, and at every later demonstration, officers used only pain compliance.

For each arrest, officers warned the demonstrators that pain compliance would be used if they did not move, that it would hurt, and that they could reduce the pain by standing up and relieving the tension on their wrists and arms. Officers then tightened the OPNs around the arrestees' wrists until they stood and walked. All arrestees complained of injuries to their hands and arms, including bruises, a pinched nerve, and one broken wrist.

Several demonstrators sued under the Fourth Amendment, claiming excessive force in the arrests and claiming that the city's pain compliance policy was itself unconstitutional. A magistrate judge found the policy constitutional and granted summary judgment to the city on that claim, but let the case go to a jury on whether any particular use of force was unconstitutional. After viewing a videotape of the arrests, the jury found that none of the arrests involved excessive force and returned a verdict for the city. The court denied a motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict, and the demonstrators appealed.
holding:
Affirmed. The court reviewed the jury's verdict only for substantial evidence, noting that whether the amount of force used was reasonable "is usually a question of fact to be determined by the jury."

The standard. The court applied Graham v. Connor: all excessive force claims arising from an arrest are analyzed under the Fourth Amendment's objective reasonableness standard, balancing the nature and quality of the intrusion against the countervailing governmental interests. Quoting its en banc decision in Hammer v. Gross, the court said the question is not simply whether the force was necessary to accomplish a legitimate police objective but "whether the force used was reasonable in light of all the relevant circumstances." In a footnote the court rejected the dissent's approach of treating the three Graham factors (severity of the crime, immediate threat, active resistance or flight) as a rigid three-part test; the inquiry is the totality of the circumstances.

The intrusion. The court found the nature and quality of the intrusion "less significant than most claims of force." Officers did not threaten or use deadly force and did not deliver blows or cuts. The force consisted only of physical pressure applied to the demonstrators' limbs in increasing degrees, resulting in pain.

The governmental interest. The city had a legitimate interest in quickly dispersing and removing lawbreakers with the least risk of injury to police and others. The arrestees were part of a group of more than 100 protesters acting in an organized effort to invade private property, obstruct business, and hinder law enforcement. Although many of the offenses were misdemeanors, the city's interest in preventing organized lawlessness was significant, and officers were justifiably concerned about risk of injury to medical staff, patients, and other protesters.

No least intrusive alternative requirement. The demonstrators argued that drag and carry was a more reasonable method and that anything else was excessive. The court rejected the premise: "Police officers, however, are not required to use the least intrusive degree of force possible." The inquiry is whether the force actually used was reasonable from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene. "Whether officers hypothetically could have used less painful, less injurious, or more effective force in executing an arrest is simply not the issue."

The evidence. Each officer had discretion whether to use force and how much. The videotape showed that after the demonstrators ignored pleas to desist and warnings about pain compliance, officers used "minimal and controlled force in a manner designed to limit injuries to all involved." In a footnote the court added that the videotape showed officers applying a loose grip first and tightening progressively until the demonstrator stood, and releasing the OPNs the moment the demonstrator complied. Substantial evidence supported the verdict.

The policy decided in advance. The demonstrators argued that only the first responding officers' conduct mattered because later officers were bound by a policy made off the scene. The court disagreed in a footnote: the chief based the policy on anticipated circumstances that matched what officers actually encountered, and if that evidence were not enough, police departments could never develop general arrest policies.

The policy's constitutionality was not decided. Because the jury found no constitutional injury, the question whether the city's policy authorized excessive force was moot under City of Los Angeles v. Heller. The court declined to award attorney's fees to either side.

The dissent. Judge Kleinfeld would have held the use of nonchakus on nonviolent, passive demonstrators unconstitutional as a matter of law. He stressed that the majority had not decided that pain compliance techniques are permissible as a matter of law, only that a jury verdict could stand, and that "the identical facts could easily have resulted in substantial damages awards" that would also have been upheld. Applying the Graham factors one by one, he found misdemeanor crimes, passive rather than active resistance, no flight, and no threat beyond the risk of back strain to officers, and he viewed the pain as punishment for refusing to walk rather than as a means of moving people, because officers still had to use pressure points, hair, and clothing to get demonstrators to the vans.
notDecided:
Whether the city's pain compliance policy was constitutional. The court expressly declined to decide this once the jury found no constitutional injury.

Whether pain compliance techniques on passive resisters are reasonable as a matter of law. The court held only that substantial evidence supported this jury's verdict on this videotape. The dissent pointed out that a verdict the other way on the same facts could also have been upheld.

Any First Amendment claim. The demonstrators sued under the Fourth Amendment only, and the dissent noted that the chief's testimony that only Operation Rescue demonstrators were subjected to the pain compliance policy raised a First Amendment question that was not before the court.

Whether drag and carry is a lawful or unlawful alternative. The court said the availability of a hypothetical alternative is not the test; it did not rule on drag and carry itself.
inPractice:
Forrester is the Ninth Circuit's anchor for using pain compliance to move a passive resister, but what carried the day was not the technique, it was the process the jury saw on video. Officers gave a verbal warning and a chance to leave, announced the arrest and gave another chance to move, told the arrestee that the hold would hurt and how to make it stop, applied pressure gradually, and released the moment the person stood. The court called that "minimal and controlled force."

The rule to carry: officers are not required to choose the least intrusive degree of force. The question is whether the force used was reasonable under all the circumstances, judged from the scene, not whether some other option might have hurt less.

The limit to carry: this was a jury verdict reviewed for substantial evidence, not a holding that pain compliance on passive resisters is always lawful. The policy's constitutionality was never decided. A different jury, or a different video, could go the other way, and the dissent said so.

Dr. Sowards teaches Forrester as the model sequence for passive resisters: commands, a warning that explains how to end the pain, time to comply, only the pain needed to move the person, release on compliance, and documentation. He also teaches that lift and carry with enough officers remains a legitimate alternative to consider, and that California's statutes enacted after 1994 ask officers to consider feasible alternatives even though the Fourth Amendment does not require the least intrusive one.
trainIt:
Run the Forrester sequence as a drill, not a lecture. Role players sit, go limp, and refuse to bear weight. The student must: identify the offense and the authority to arrest; give a clear command and a chance to comply; announce the arrest; give a second chance to move; state that pain compliance is coming, that it will hurt, and exactly what the person can do to stop it; apply the hold gradually; and release on the first sign of compliance. Debrief against the phrase the court used: minimal and controlled force designed to limit injuries to all involved.

Teach the injury profile honestly. Even with warnings and gradual pressure, the record included bruises, a pinched nerve, and a broken wrist. Wrist holds and OPNs load the wrist joint; students must know the anatomy they are stressing and must stop increasing pressure once the person begins to rise.

Teach the alternatives question correctly. The Fourth Amendment does not require the least intrusive option, so an officer who chose a pain compliance hold is not wrong just because a lift and carry was possible. But the reasonableness analysis still considers the totality, and California policy and statute ask officers to think about feasible alternatives. Practice articulating why the chosen technique fit the scene: crowd size, number of officers, injury risk to officers and arrestees, and the need to move quickly.

Teach the posture: a jury verdict affirmed, the policy question left open, and a dissent that would have gone the other way as a matter of law. Students should be able to explain why that matters when they write a report that will be judged by a jury watching video.
caution: The opinion was read in full from the Public.Resource.Org archive. Pin cites are not given because the archive text has no reporter page breaks. The facts are as the Ninth Circuit summarized the trial record. The holding is an affirmance of a jury verdict on substantial evidence review and should not be taught as a holding that pain compliance on passive resisters is lawful as a matter of law.
dissent: Judge Kleinfeld dissented. He would have held that using nonchakus to inflict pain on nonviolent, passive demonstrators was unconstitutional as a matter of law because it was both ineffective and unnecessarily brutal. He applied the Graham factors individually: the crimes were misdemeanor trespass and failure to disperse; the demonstrators resisted passively, not actively, and did not flee; and the only safety concern was back strain to officers who had to lift them, which he said could be addressed by assigning more or larger officers. He read the record as showing that the pain did not get people to walk, so officers still had to use pressure points, hair, and clothing to move them, which made the pain punishment rather than a means of arrest. He also warned municipal officials not to read the majority as approving pain compliance on demonstrators, because the majority only let a jury verdict stand. The majority answered in footnotes that his analysis was hindsight, that the video showed gradual application and release on compliance, and that his view would make it impossible for departments to adopt general arrest policies.

applications.title: Warn in a way that gives the person a way out
applications.body: The officers in Forrester did more than announce force. They told each demonstrator that the hold would hurt and that standing up would end the pain. That instruction converted the hold from punishment into a choice, and the court relied on it.

applications.title: Gradual on, immediate off
applications.body: The majority's footnote describes a loose grip tightened progressively and released the moment the demonstrator complied. That is the technique standard the court approved. Continuing pressure after the person starts to rise is the behavior the dissent called punishment.

applications.title: You do not have to pick the gentlest option
applications.body: Officers are not required to use the least intrusive degree of force possible. Whether a less painful or more effective method existed is not the issue. The issue is whether what was done was reasonable under all the circumstances, viewed from the scene.

applications.title: Video decides these cases
applications.body: The jury watched the entire videotape and excerpts repeatedly. The court said the video removed much argument about the facts. Assume every pain compliance arrest will be judged by people watching it frame by frame.

applications.title: Do not oversell the case
applications.body: Forrester affirmed a jury verdict. It did not hold that pain compliance on passive resisters is constitutional as a matter of law and it did not decide whether the city's policy was lawful. Teach it as a case about process and evidence, not as blanket permission.

quiz.q: What did the Ninth Circuit hold in Forrester about alternatives to the force an officer chooses?
options: Officers must use the least intrusive degree of force available
Officers are not required to use the least intrusive degree of force; the question is whether the force used was reasonable under all the circumstances
Officers must always try drag and carry before pain compliance
Alternatives are irrelevant and may never be considered
quiz.teach: The court said whether officers hypothetically could have used less painful, less injurious, or more effective force is simply not the issue. Alternatives are part of the totality, but the Fourth Amendment does not demand the least intrusive one.

quiz.q: What was the procedural result in Forrester?
options: The court held pain compliance techniques constitutional as a matter of law
The court held the city's pain compliance policy constitutional
The court affirmed a jury verdict for the city on substantial evidence review and declined to decide whether the policy was constitutional
The court reversed and ordered a new trial
quiz.teach: This was substantial evidence review of a jury verdict. Once the jury found no constitutional injury, the policy question was moot under City of Los Angeles v. Heller. The dissent stressed that the same facts could have supported a verdict the other way.

quiz.q: Which fact did the court rely on in finding the force minimal and controlled?
options: Officers carried the demonstrators to the vans
Officers applied the OPNs loosely, tightened gradually, and released as soon as the demonstrator stood
quiz.teach: The record included bruises, a pinched nerve, and a broken wrist, and the offenses were misdemeanors. What the court credited was the warning, the gradual application, and release on compliance shown on the videotape.
